messages.author: c9eec36a3a9e119a
messages.subject: Using dsm without coordinates?
parts:
Hi all-

I may be way off base here, but much head scratching and research has led me to seek the advice from this wise group.


Basic background:

Fish count data (with covariates) from line transect sampling via manned submersible.

Detection probability functions were already fit incorporating variables (primary substrate type and depth) determined to affect the detection of rockfish using MCDS in R.

Ultimately, our end goal is to create a quantitative predictive model for density incorporating the variables determined to affect detection (the number one variable is primary substrate type, for example).  I feel as if DSM would be the ideal approach to meet this objective, however, we don't have coordinate readings at the level of observations (only the start/end of the transect).  We do have total transect length and constant speed, so I was able to estimate m/s accumulative distance traveled .  I then calculated the area sizes (of substrate type) as we moved along the transect, thinking this would suffice as my segments. Obviously these segments aren't uniform in length/size. Problem?

Main question/problem: can this analysis even be done without the coordinates? 
Any suggestions for alternatives?  I keep scratching my head thinking of how I can tie together all of these pieces I have.

I hope this relatively clear to understand! I truly appreciate any help and/or suggestions. Something about bringing this all together just isn't clicking for me!

Thanks!

messages.author: 9b03386432b784c0
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Using dsm without coordinates?
parts:
Hi Katy, list

DSM is not really my thing, but here are some comments. Hope I didn't miss the point entirely ;)

You do not need the coordinates of the individuals per se. But you need some minimal data related to location. You don't have the coordinates for each observation, but I assume you can put them into "boxes" (i.e. transect segments) given your constant speed? If that is the case then you should be able to implement a DSM, since the spatial modelling happens at the "box" level, not at the individual observation level. The only modelling that goes on at the individual level is regarding detectability, but for that I assume you have the relevant covariates for each observation.

I also assume you have the habitat covariate (and any other(s) going into the DSM) over the entire area you might want your inferences to apply to? As that would be required for the prediction stage, i.e. naturally you do not need the covariates for the DSM on the transects only, but everywhere else.

People have typically used equal size boxes to do the modelling, but I don't see why one might not use unequal size boxes (if say, because, as in your case, useful covariates to explain density appear in discrete patches) as long as due care is taken regarding properly accounting for the size of the box via the offset. There might be unforeseen problems if some boxes are much larger than others. Also not sure if the existing packages to implement DSMs can deal with that off the shelf or would you have to tweak them / code it yourself.

Hope this helps, but DSM folks might have more ideas/thoughts

cheers

Tiago

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Using dsm without coordinates?
parts:
Katy

Dr. Marques has provided good answers to your questions.  Just to amplify a couple of points.

As Tiago says, your effort needs to be defined at the segment (hist term 'box') level.  The key point is that you are able to properly assign your detections to the segment in which it belongs. But segments need not be of the same length.  I would avoid making segments very short, because detections made in these small segments will have a large influence upon your DSM.

Also as Tiago pointed out, to perform prediction using the results from a fitted DSM, you will need covariate values for the entire study area.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Using dsm without coordinates?
parts:
Katy

You know the address of this list when you have more questions.

The concept of segmentation is that "effort" is being segmented, not the environment.  Imagine you were doing a survey for cetaceans from a surface ship (a very common use of DSMs).  You don't know where on the surface of the ocean the 'habitat' changes; the 'habitat' variables are continuous, such as sea surface temperature or prey density.  Consequently you cannot perform segmentation upon changing habitat.  Instead the survey effort is segmented.

I'm afraid the 'flatfile' approach will not be applicable for your density surface model analysis.  That is because the hierarchical data structure needed for density surface modelling (because of segments nested within transects and observations within segments) is not accommodated by the 'flatfile' data format.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Using dsm without coordinates?
parts:
Katy

If your interest is in estimating fish density using distance sampling, you need not use density surface modelling.  Conventional distance sampling quite happily can produce density estimates taking into account sources of variation in detectability caused by various factors you mentioned.

Density surface modelling attempts to estimate differences in animal density related to environmental covariates.  The covariates are spatially referenced, as are the animal locations.  Density surface models model the relationship between counts (adjusted for incomplete detectability) and the covariates using the locations (coordinates) of both to establish the correspondence of the two types of data.  Without animal locations the modelling process cannot succeed.  It is very much the case that knowing the manner in which data are to be analysed needs to be considered prior to the collection data.
